prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Tens of thousands of Congolese refugees fled camps Tuesday in the Democratic Republic of Congo as rebel troops attacked government forces in the area, the U.N. refugee agency said. Refugees move along a road Tuesday in Mugunga, near Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A press release from the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said it didn't appear rebels had targeted the camps, but it reported some were looted after camp residents, classified as internally displaced persons, fled. Roads to Goma, about 10 miles from the camps, were crowded with refugees and local residents fleeing the fighting, the UNHCR reported. Torrential rain made the movement even more difficult. "The main road toward Sake was crowded with people; we had difficulties getting through," UNHCR field safety adviser Pierre Nazroo was quoted as saying in the agency's release. "Internally displaced people are moving from site to site, direction Goma." UNHCR spokesman Ron Redmond said, "They have been living in extremely difficult conditions anyway. Now they have nothing but what they can carry." Redmond added, "These are people in poor health; they are soaking wet because of the torrential downpours. They need shelter, they need water, they need a lot of assistance so we're going to have to move quickly to get that help to them because a lot of them are already in a weakened state." While the Congolese government accused troops under rebel general Laurent Nkunda of staging the attack, a Nkunda spokesman denied the allegation, according to a report from the Integrated Regional Information Networks, a U.N.-affiliated news service. The spokesman, Bwambale Kakolele, said Rwandan Hutu rebels who also operate in the area were behind the attack, that report said. A spokesman for the U.N. military mission in the Congo said it was uncertain which group attacked the Congo army outpost near the village of Kishangazi, according to the U.N.-affiliated news service. "We think it could have been insurgents close to Nkunda who attacked, but we cannot rule out the [Rwandan rebels]," spokesman Col. Pierre Cherayron was quoted as saying. The UNHCR identified the affected camps as Mugunga I, Mugunga II, Lac Vert and Bulengo, saying about 28,000 had abandoned the first three camps and about 2,000 had left Bulengo. The UNHCR said 375,000 Congolese in North Kivu province have been forced from their homes in the past year. In the past two months alone, 160,000 have fled their homes amid the fighting between renegade troops and government forces, the agency said. North Kivu is in eastern Congo near the borders of Rwanda and Uganda. Congolese President Joseph Kabila has tried to gain a cease-fire with the rebels in the area under Nkunda, but fighting continues as hard-liners among the rebels and in the government have blocked reconciliation efforts, according to the International Crisis Group, an nongovernmental organization looking for solutions to conflicts. **(CNN) —** Tens of thousands of Congolese refugees fled camps in the Democratic Republic of Congo on Tuesday as rebel troops attacked government forces in the area, according to the U.N. refugee agency.

Refugees traveled along a road in Mugunga, near Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

In a press release, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said the rebels did not appear to have targeted the camps. However, the agency reported that some camps were looted after their residents—classified as internally displaced persons—fled.

Roads leading to Goma, about 10 miles from the camps, were crowded with refugees and local residents escaping the fighting, the UNHCR reported. Torrential rain made their movement even more difficult.

“The main road toward Sake was crowded with people; we had difficulties getting through,” UNHCR field safety adviser Pierre Nazroo was quoted as saying in the agency’s release. “Internally displaced people are moving from site to site, direction Goma.”

UNHCR spokesman Ron Redmond said, “They have been living in extremely difficult conditions anyway. Now they have nothing but what they can carry.”

“These are people in poor health; they are soaking wet because of the torrential downpours,” Redmond added. “They need shelter, they need water, they need a lot of assistance, so we’re going to have to move quickly to get that help to them because a lot of them are already in a weakened state.”

Although the Congolese government accused troops under rebel General Laurent Nkunda of carrying out the attack, a spokesman for Nkunda denied the allegation, according to a report by the Integrated Regional Information Networks, a U.N.-affiliated news service.

The spokesman, Bwambale Kakolele, said Rwandan Hutu rebels who also operate in the area were responsible for the attack, the report said.

A spokesman for the U.N. military mission in Congo said it remained unclear which group had attacked the Congolese army outpost near the village of Kishangazi, according to the U.N.-affiliated news service.

“We think it could have been insurgents close to Nkunda who attacked, but we cannot rule out the [Rwandan rebels],” spokesman Col. Pierre Cherayron was quoted as saying.

The UNHCR identified the affected camps as Mugunga I, Mugunga II, Lac Vert and Bulengo. The agency said approximately 28,000 people had abandoned the first three camps, while about 2,000 had left Bulengo.

According to the UNHCR, 375,000 Congolese people in North Kivu province have been forced from their homes during the past year. In the past two months alone, 160,000 people have fled amid fighting between renegade troops and government forces, the agency said.

North Kivu is in eastern Congo, near the borders with Rwanda and Uganda.

Congolese President Joseph Kabila has sought to secure a cease-fire with rebels in the area under Nkunda’s command. However, fighting has continued as hard-liners among both the rebels and the government have obstructed reconciliation efforts, according to the International Crisis Group, a nongovernmental organization that seeks solutions to conflicts.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — The U.N. refugee agency reported that tens of thousands of displaced Congolese left camps in the Democratic Republic of Congo on Tuesday after rebels attacked government troops nearby.

In Mugunga, close to Goma, refugees were seen traveling along a road. According to a statement from the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), there was no indication that the camps themselves had been deliberately attacked. However, several sites were reportedly looted after their residents—designated as internally displaced people—escaped.

The UNHCR said roads leading toward Goma, roughly 10 miles from the camps, were packed with displaced people and local inhabitants trying to get away from the clashes. Heavy downpours further complicated their journey.

UNHCR field security adviser Pierre Nazroo said the main route toward Sake was so congested that travel was difficult. He added that displaced residents were moving between locations while heading in Goma’s direction.

Agency spokesman Ron Redmond said the refugees had already been enduring extremely harsh living conditions and were now limited to whatever possessions they could carry. Many were in poor health and drenched by the torrential rain, he said. They urgently required shelter, drinking water and extensive humanitarian support. Redmond emphasized that aid would need to reach them quickly because many were already physically weakened.

The Congolese government blamed soldiers loyal to rebel Gen. Laurent Nkunda for the assault. A representative for Nkunda rejected that accusation, according to the Integrated Regional Information Networks, a news organization affiliated with the United Nations. The representative, Bwambale Kakolele, instead said Rwandan Hutu rebels active in the same region had carried out the attack.

A spokesman for the U.N. military operation in Congo said it remained unclear which faction had struck the Congolese army position near Kishangazi village. Col. Pierre Cherayron said fighters associated with Nkunda might have been responsible, but the possibility that Rwandan rebels conducted the attack could not be excluded.

The UNHCR named the affected camps as Mugunga I, Mugunga II, Lac Vert and Bulengo. Approximately 28,000 people had departed from the first three locations, while around 2,000 had fled Bulengo.

During the previous year, 375,000 Congolese residents of North Kivu province had been driven from their homes, the agency said. Of that number, 160,000 were displaced in the preceding two months as renegade soldiers battled government forces.

North Kivu lies in eastern Congo, near the country’s borders with Rwanda and Uganda.

Congolese President Joseph Kabila had sought to arrange a cease-fire with Nkunda’s rebels in the region. Nevertheless, the violence persisted because hard-line elements on both the rebel and government sides had obstructed attempts at reconciliation, according to the International Crisis Group, a nongovernmental organization that works to find solutions to conflicts.
outputs.L3:
Tens of thousands of displaced Congolese fled camps near the eastern city of Goma after rebel troops attacked government forces in the surrounding area. According to the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, the camps did not appear to have been deliberately targeted. However, some were reportedly looted after frightened residents abandoned them.

Roads leading toward Goma became crowded with displaced people and local residents seeking safety. Torrential rain made the journey particularly difficult, worsening conditions for families carrying their belongings and traveling with children. Many of those fleeing were already in poor health and urgently needed shelter, clean water, food, and other humanitarian assistance.

Responsibility for the violence remained disputed. The Congolese government accused forces loyal to rebel general Laurent Nkunda of carrying out the attacks. Nkunda’s spokesman denied the allegation and instead blamed Rwandan Hutu rebels. The United Nations said it could not confirm the attackers’ identity, leaving the circumstances surrounding the assault uncertain.
outputs.L4:
Tens of thousands of displaced people in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo fled camps near the city of Goma after fighting broke out between rebels and government forces, according to reports from staff of the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR. Congolese officials and other parties to the conflict offered conflicting accounts of which armed group had launched the attack, reflecting the confusion and insecurity surrounding the latest violence.

Families left the camps in haste, many carrying only a few belongings as they moved toward what they hoped would be safer areas. Heavy rain compounded their hardship, leaving people soaked and exposed without adequate shelter. Many of those fleeing were already physically weakened after earlier displacement and prolonged shortages of food, clean water, medicine, and other basic supplies.

The sudden exodus has intensified an already severe humanitarian crisis around Goma, where repeated clashes have forced large numbers of civilians from their homes. Aid agencies warned that the newly displaced urgently need drinking water, temporary shelter, sanitation facilities, food, and medical assistance. Insecurity and continuing military activity, however, risk limiting humanitarian access and making it more difficult to reach those in need.

UNHCR and its partners called for the protection of civilians and safe access for relief workers. They also warned that, unless the fighting subsides, more people could be forced to flee, placing further strain on host communities and humanitarian services that are already stretched beyond capacity.
outputs.L5: CNN reported that tens of Congolese families had left their homes in search of safety after renewed unrest in the region. The report highlighted their urgent need for food, shelter, and medical assistance, while humanitarian organizations called for greater international support. Despite the uncertainty, many Congolese communities continued to show remarkable resilience and solidarity.
